candidates.quote: The purpose of life is not to be happy. It is to be useful, to be honorable, to be compassionate, to have it make some difference that you have lived and lived well.
candidates.trueOrigin: Leo Calvin Rosten, 1962 National Book Awards address
candidates.whyNotable: Widely circulated as Emerson's; Wikiquote traces it to Leo Rosten's remarks at the 1962 National Book Awards ('not to be happy — but to matter').

candidates.quote: What lies behind us and what lies ahead of us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry Stanley Haskins, Meditations in Wall Street (1940)
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Emerson lines on graduation cards and social media; Wikiquote traces it to Henry Stanley Haskins' 1940 book Meditations in Wall Street, whose author was initially anonymous, making a prestige name like Emerson attractive.

candidates.quote: The secret of change is to focus all of your energy, not on fighting the old, but on building the new.
candidates.trueOrigin: Dan Millman, Way of the Peaceful Warrior (1980)
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of motivational posters pinned on Socrates; QI shows it was spoken by a fictional character named Socrates in Dan Millman's 1980 novel Way of the Peaceful Warrior.

candidates.quote: My girlfriend always laughs during sex — no matter what she's reading.
candidates.trueOrigin: A stand-up joke by comedian Emo Philips, misattributed to Jobs as it spread online. Jobs has no connection to it.
candidates.whyNotable: A striking example of internet quote-drift — a comedian's one-liner absurdly pinned on Jobs; Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed.

candidates.quote: A government big enough to give you everything you want is a government big enough to take from you everything you have.
candidates.trueOrigin: President Gerald Ford, address to a joint session of Congress, 1974
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-forwarded small-government quotes; Wikiquote attributes it to President Gerald Ford's 1974 address to Congress, not Jefferson.

candidates.quote: Dissent is the highest form of patriotism.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Jefferson; earliest documented appearance in a 1961 Quaker publication, popularized in the 1960s
candidates.whyNotable: A protest-movement staple pinned on Jefferson with no source; Wikiquote traces it to a 1961 Quaker publication, popularized in the 1960s (associated with Howard Zinn).

candidates.quote: The democracy will cease to exist when you take away from those who are willing to work and give to those who would not.
candidates.trueOrigin: From the 1986 book Dreams Come Due, written under the pseudonym "John Galt"
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely circulated political meme; Wikiquote traces it to the 1986 book Dreams Come Due, written under the pseudonym "John Galt" — not Jefferson at all.

candidates.quote: To learn who rules over you, simply find out who you are not allowed to criticize
candidates.trueOrigin: Kevin Alfred Strom, 1993
candidates.whyNotable: A viral political meme constantly captioned 'Voltaire' that Wikiquote traces to a 1993 essay by white-nationalist Kevin Alfred Strom, not Voltaire at all.

candidates.quote: If you can dream it, you can do it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Tom Fitzgerald, a Disney Imagineer, who wrote it specifically for the Horizons attraction at Epcot (opened 1983); confirmed by Disney archivist Dave Smith.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-pinned inspirational lines on Disney; Wikiquote documents that Imagineer Tom Fitzgerald wrote it for Epcot's Horizons attraction and confirmed 'I wrote it!'

candidates.quote: You can't just let nature run wild.
candidates.trueOrigin: Walter Joseph Hickel, U.S. Secretary of the Interior, regarding wolf killing, as quoted in Living With Wolves (2005) by James Dutcher, p. 8.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently circulated as a Disney line, but Wikiquote traces it to Interior Secretary Walter J. Hickel speaking about wolf killing, not Disney.

candidates.quote: A penny saved is a penny earned
candidates.trueOrigin: A reworded popular paraphrase; Franklin's genuine 1737 Poor Richard's line was 'A penny saved is two pence clear,' and the 'penny saved is a penny got' form predates Franklin.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted 'Franklin' thrift maxim, but it is a modern paraphrase; his actual Poor Richard's wording was 'A penny saved is two pence clear' (and the earlier 'A penny sav'd is a penny got' predates him).

candidates.quote: The horse is here to stay, but the automobile is only a novelty — a fad.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to the president of the Michigan Savings Bank advising Ford's lawyer Horace Rackham against investing in Ford (c.1903), per Bushnell's 1922 biography.
candidates.whyNotable: Often retold as a prediction about (or even by) Ford's world; QI shows it was a warning made by a banker to Ford's lawyer circa 1903, documented in Sarah Bushnell's 1922 Ford biography — not a Ford quote.

candidates.quote: Live as if you were to die tomorrow. Learn as if you were to live forever.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ancient/medieval aphorism (echoes the Hitopadesha and is attributed to Isidore of Seville, c. 560-636, in the FPA Book of Quotations, 1952, among others); no Gandhi source.
candidates.whyNotable: A graduation-card favorite credited to Gandhi, but Wikiquote documents the aphorism circulating for centuries — attributed variously to Isidore of Seville, Edmund Rich, Alain de Lille and Erasmus — long before Gandhi.

candidates.quote: The greatness of a nation and its moral progress can be judged by the way its animals are treated.
candidates.trueOrigin: David Strauss, The Old Faith and the New (Der alte und der neue Glaube, 1872): 'The manner in which a nation in the aggregate treats animals, is one chief measure of its real civilization.' Attributed to Gandhi since at least 1980.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous in animal-welfare and vegetarian circles, but Wikiquote finds it in none of Gandhi's Complete Works; the original is by German theologian David Strauss (1872).

candidates.quote: What you do speaks so loudly that I cannot hear what you say.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase of Ralph Waldo Emerson, 'Social Aims' in Letters and Social Aims (1875)
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely rooted in Emerson but not in this form; QI shows the popular one-liner is an abridged, simplified rewrite of what Emerson actually wrote in 'Social Aims.'

candidates.quote: Contentment is natural wealth, luxury is artificial poverty.
candidates.trueOrigin: Source unknown; appears in Charles Simmons' A Laconic Manual (1852) without attribution
candidates.whyNotable: Circulated as a Socrates aphorism but Wikiquote lists it under Attributed with no original source — it appears in Charles Simmons' 1852 manual with no classical citation.

candidates.quote: I know that I know nothing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase/back-translation of Plato's Apology 21d and Republic 354b-c
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive 'Socratic paradox' — hugely famous but Wikiquote flags the pithy wording as a modern back-translation; it derives loosely from Plato's Apology 21d rather than being a literal quotation.

candidates.quote: History is but a fable agreed upon
candidates.trueOrigin: Voltaire, Jeannot et Colin (1764), spoken by a character crediting an unnamed wit
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely traceable to Voltaire's 1764 tale Jeannot et Colin, but QI notes he put the line in a character's mouth crediting an unnamed wit, so the direct attribution is imprecise.

candidates.quote: You don't have to be crazy to work here, but it helps.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous comedic template ('You don't have to be X to Y but it helps') documented from June 1920, over a decade before it was attributed to Disney.
candidates.whyNotable: Credited to Disney via his secretary in a 1933 newspaper, but QI shows it is a 'snowclone' joke template with anonymous instances dating to 1920, so Disney did not originate it.

candidates.quote: I will send a barrel of this wonderful whiskey to every general in the army.
candidates.trueOrigin: An anecdote about Grant's drinking printed anonymously in 1863 newspapers; QI notes it mirrors an older King George II / General Wolfe story and that aide Thomas Eckert said Lincoln denied it. Evidence is inconclusive.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous Civil War Lincoln witticism that QI concludes cannot be solidly confirmed or refuted, likely templated on an 18th-century royal anecdote.

candidates.quote: You can fool all the people some of the time, and some of the people all the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time.
candidates.trueOrigin: No contemporaneous record exists; earliest attribution to Lincoln is an 1885 letter by prohibitionist H. Clay Bascom, two decades after Lincoln's death. Also credited to P. T. Barnum.
candidates.whyNotable: Perhaps the single most-quoted 'Lincoln' aphorism, yet QI finds no evidence he ever said it and the phrase only appears in the 1880s.

candidates.quote: Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase via Roger Sessions (NYT, 1950) and Louis Zukofsky (Poetry, 1950); loosely based on Einstein's 1933 Oxford lecture.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitously quoted as Einstein but QI shows the pithy wording is a paraphrase: composer Roger Sessions attributed an 'in effect' version to Einstein in a 1950 New York Times piece, popularized by poet Louis Zukofsky the same year; Einstein's genuine 1933 Oxford lecture expressed the idea far more verbosely.

candidates.quote: Two things are infinite: the universe and human stupidity; and I'm not sure about the universe
candidates.trueOrigin: Frederick (Fritz) Perls, 'Ego, Hunger, and Aggression' (1947); Einstein credit added by Perls in 1969, unverifiable.
candidates.whyNotable: A clever line constantly pinned on Einstein; QI shows it rests entirely on Gestalt therapist Fritz Perls, who first published a version in 1947 crediting 'a great astronomer' and only named Einstein in 1969, with the wording mutating across his books.

candidates.quote: Happiness depends upon ourselves.
candidates.trueOrigin: Translator's gloss by J. A. K. Thomson, The Ethics of Aristotle (1955); not in the original Greek
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates as a tidy Aristotle aphorism; Wikiquote notes it is an interpretive gloss added by translator J. A. K. Thomson (1955) and does not appear in the original Greek at 1099b.29.

candidates.quote: It is the mark of an educated mind to be able to entertain a thought without accepting it.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Aristotelian source; unattributed modern paraphrase
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous 'critical thinking' meme credited to Aristotle; Wikiquote lists it as disputed with no genuine source, possibly a garbling of Nicomachean Ethics 1094b.24.

candidates.quote: If you think you are too small to make a difference, try sleeping with a mosquito.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest documented use attributed to Anita Roddick (Time, Jan 1993); no genuine Dalai Lama source, often relabeled an African proverb.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitously captioned as a Dalai Lama or 'African proverb' line, but Wikiquote's earliest trace is a 1993 Time magazine attribution to Anita Roddick, with Dalai Lama credits only appearing from 2004.

candidates.quote: Don't cry because it's over. Smile because it happened.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Seuss (d. 1991) ever said it; assigned to him by 2002. Also credited over the years to Ludwig Jacobowski (1899) and Gabriel Garcia Marquez; QI finds no solid attribution.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Seuss lines; Quote Investigator finds no substantive link to Seuss and traces the Seuss credit only to about 2002.

candidates.quote: A woman is like a tea bag; you never know how strong it is until it's in hot water.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Roosevelt source; a similar remark was attributed to Nancy Reagan in 1981.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral 'empowerment' line constantly credited to Roosevelt, but Wikiquote finds no original source and notes a closely related quip attributed to Nancy Reagan in 1981.

candidates.quote: Yesterday is history, tomorrow is a mystery, and today is a gift, that's why they call it the present.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified originator; QI documents anonymous earlier variants of the 'present/gift' wordplay with no link to Roosevelt.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous inspirational line attributed to Roosevelt (and others, e.g. Kung Fu Panda); QI finds no genuine Roosevelt source and traces the saying to anonymous earlier wordplay.

candidates.quote: You must learn from the mistakes of others. You can't possibly live long enough to make them all yourself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous folk saying circulating by the 1940s; the attribution to Roosevelt appeared much later.
candidates.whyNotable: Folk-wisdom aphorism attributed to Roosevelt, but QI traces it to 1940s sources circulating without her name and finds the Roosevelt ascription is a later addition.

candidates.quote: All things are subject to interpretation; whichever interpretation prevails at a given time is a function of power and not the truth.
candidates.trueOrigin: Loosely paraphrases a note from Nietzsche's 1888 Nachlass, but the specific 'function of power' wording is not his; commonly circulated without citation.
candidates.whyNotable: Very widely quoted as Nietzsche, but Wikiquote notes it is usually cited without a source and the closest real passage does not mention 'power'.

candidates.quote: When we are tired, we are attacked by ideas we conquered long ago.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attribution to Nietzsche unverified; QI located no supporting citation in his works.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely attributed to Nietzsche, but QI is skeptical — no solid citation to a specific work has been found.

candidates.quote: It is too probable that no plan we propose will be adopted. Perhaps another dreadful conflict is to be sustained.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Washington at the Constitutional Convention (25 May 1787) but uncorroborated in Madison's notes; authenticity contested (Bancroft accepted it, Lodge argued against).
candidates.whyNotable: Inscribed at the Department of Commerce, the Washington Square arch, and Constitution Hall as Washington's words at the 1787 Constitutional Convention, yet it is absent from Madison's convention records and rejected by historians like Henry Cabot Lodge.

candidates.quote: It is well enough that people of the nation do not understand our banking and monetary system, for if they did, I believe there would be a revolution before tomorrow morning.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase introduced by Rep. Charles Binderup (1937); no direct Ford source, though Ford wrote against finance dominance in My Life and Work.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial conspiracy/finance meme attributed to Ford; Wikiquote notes it originates as a 1937 paraphrase by Congressman Charles Binderup, not a documented Ford quote.

candidates.quote: I like your Christ. I do not like your Christians. Your Christians are so unlike your Christ.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Gandhi source located; nearest documented antecedent is Bara Dada in E. Stanley Jones, The Christ of the Indian Road (1925): 'Jesus is ideal and wonderful, but you Christians -- you are not like him.'
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly quoted in sermons and Christian apologetics, but Wikiquote finds no source in Gandhi's works; a very similar line is attributed to 'Bara Dada' in E. Stanley Jones's The Christ of the Indian Road (1925).

candidates.quote: I think it would be a good idea.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apocryphal; earliest located attribution is a 1967 CBS News documentary 'The Italians' (per Reader's Digest 1967), popularized via E. F. Schumacher's Good Work (1979).
candidates.whyNotable: The famous quip supposedly given when Gandhi was asked what he thought of Western civilization; QI shows the earliest source is a 1967 CBS documentary nearly 20 years after his death, with no film or biographical record of him saying it.

candidates.quote: But suppose the child inherited my beauty and your brains?
candidates.trueOrigin: A floating joke that predates Monroe by decades, told earlier about George Bernard Shaw, Isadora Duncan, and others.
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'beauty and brains' comeback (often set as a Monroe-and-Einstein or Monroe-and-Bernard-Shaw exchange); QI shows the joke circulated long before Monroe and is a floating anecdote.

candidates.quote: There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics.
candidates.trueOrigin: Twain attributed it to Benjamin Disraeli; actual coiner is unconfirmed (various late-19th-century candidates).
candidates.whyNotable: Twain popularized and helped spread this line but himself credited it to Benjamin Disraeli; the true originator remains disputed.

candidates.quote: The old law of an eye for an eye leaves everybody blind.
candidates.trueOrigin: Proverb of indefinite origin, variously attributed to Gandhi and others; no verified King source.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely credited to King (and used in Spike Lee's 'Do the Right Thing') but the underlying 'eye for an eye leaves everybody blind' proverb has no firm origin and is also pinned on Gandhi.

candidates.quote: To be a Christian without prayer is no more possible than to be alive without breathing.
candidates.trueOrigin: First attributed to King by George Sweeting (Moody Church) in 1979; no earlier documentation.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared as King, but Wikiquote finds no source earlier than pastor George Sweeting's 1979 book, casting doubt on the attribution.

candidates.quote: Poetry is music written for the human voice.
candidates.trueOrigin: Angelou attributed it to her mentor Bertha Flowers, not to herself.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently attributed to Angelou, but she herself credited the expression to her mentor Bertha Flowers, so the popular attribution is a reassignment.

candidates.quote: There is not a single citizen in South Africa who is not ready to stand by his Palestinian brothers in their legitimate fight against the Zionist racists.
